title: Quantum Computers
objective: After this level you can explain what makes quantum computers different, without the hype.
summary: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix until measured. Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs like simulating molecules, not replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

cards.headline: In 2019, a quantum computer did a job in 200 seconds. The argument took longer.
cards.body: Google researchers reported that their Sycamore processor finished a calculation in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a top supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM researchers replied that a better classical method could do it in 2.5 days. To judge claims like these, you need to know what a qubit is, and what it's good for.

cards.headline: A switch that isn't just on or off
cards.body: Remember Level 4's switch: open or closed, never both. An ordinary computer bit is the same, either 0 or 1. A qubit, a quantum bit, can be 0, 1 or a mix of the two, called a superposition. But the moment you measure it, you get a plain 0 or 1. The in-between only lasts until you look.

cards.headline: What they're good for
cards.body: Quantum computers aren't faster at everything. NIST expects them to help with particular problems, such as simulating the quantum rules that govern molecules, chemicals and materials. In 1994, Peter Shor described a quantum algorithm that could quickly factor the huge numbers that protect much of today's encryption. That's why, in August 2024, NIST released its first encryption standards designed to withstand quantum attacks.

cards.headline: What they're not
cards.body: A quantum computer isn't a faster laptop: NIST sees the two kinds of machine working together, not one replacing the other. Qubits are fragile. Many must be kept near absolute zero, and today's machines make an error roughly once in every thousand operations. And that 2019 task? It was a benchmark, sampling random quantum circuits, chosen because it gets exponentially harder for ordinary computers.

mascot.line: When a headline says quantum, ask: which problem, and compared with what?

questions.prompt: Why must many quantum computers be kept near absolute zero?

options.label: To stop the laptop inside from overheating
options.rationale: There's no laptop inside; qubits are the issue.

options.label: Because Level 4's switches only work when cold
options.rationale: Ordinary switches work at room temperature.

questions.explanation: Qubits are fragile and error-prone, so many designs must be kept at temperatures near absolute zero.

options.label: Simulating how molecules and materials behave

options.rationale: NIST expects the two to work together.

options.label: Storing photos with fewer errors
options.rationale: Qubits make far more errors than ordinary bits.
